title: Saying "no": prefixes that switch and an -a ending that becomes -i
goal: Negate any sentence, decline politely, and order a drink at a roadside stall without having to fall back on English.
bekal: the six negative prefixes: *si-, hu-, ha-, hatu-, ham-, hawa-*
the ending rule: verbs ending in *-a* change to *-i* when negated
the Arabic loan verbs whose endings never change

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Kwenye kibanda cha chai
dialogs.intro: Morning at a roadside tea stall. Budi tries to order by himself for the first time.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: Sorry, I don't understand. Please speak slowly.

lines.speaker: Muuzaji:
lines.id: Oh, sorry about that! Do you want tea or coffee?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: I'd like tea, please. I don't like coffee.

lines.speaker: Muuzaji:
lines.id: How much sugar do you want (spoonfuls)?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: None, thank you. I don't want any sugar at all.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Samahani, sina pesa ndogo. Nina elfu tano.
lines.id: Sorry, I don't have small change. I have five thousand.
lines.literal: sorry, I-don't-have money small. I-have thousand five.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Asante. Rafiki yangu haji leo, anaumwa.
lines.id: Thanks. My friend isn't coming today, he's sick.
lines.literal: thanks. friend of-me he-doesn't-come today, he-is-being-hurt.

lines.speaker: Muuzaji:
lines.id: So sorry to hear it. Doesn't he drink tea?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Hanywi chai, lakini anapenda maji ya matunda.
lines.id: He doesn't drink tea, but he likes fruit juice.
lines.literal: he-doesn't-drink tea, but he-is-liking water of fruits.

notes: **Pole and samahani are not two words for the same thing.** *Samahani* is used when you are at fault or want to say "excuse me". *Pole* is said to someone who is having a hard time — ill, tired, has lost something. The vendor in this dialogue says *pole* out of sympathy, not because he feels guilty.

**Sawa means "equal", and is used for "okay".** It is one of the words you hear most in East Africa. *Sawa sawa* (doubled) means "all good, no worries", and *sawa?* with a rising tone means "agreed?".
**Kabisa means "completely" and strengthens a negative.** *Sitaki* = I don't want; *sitaki kabisa* = I don't want it at all. On its own, *kabisa!* means "absolutely!".

**Maji ya matunda literally means "water of fruits" — that is juice.** Swahili often links two nouns with *ya*/*wa*/*cha* rather than inventing a new word: *maji ya matunda* (juice), *chai ya maziwa* (milk tea), *kibanda cha chai* (tea stall).

**Anaumwa means "he/she is sick", literally "he/she is being hurt".** This form is taken apart in unit 19 along with all the body vocabulary; for now learn *ninaumwa* (I am sick) and *anaumwa* (he/she is sick) as whole sentences.

grammars.title: Negation: two things change at once
body: Negating a present-tense sentence in Swahili changes **two** things at once, and the *-na-* slot actually disappears:
**(1)** the subject prefix is replaced by a negative prefix, and **(2)** the final *-a* of the verb changes to *-i*.
after: The *-na-* slot is dropped because its job is done: this negative covers "isn't doing" and "doesn't usually do" at once. *Sisomi* means "I'm not reading" **and** "I never read", depending on context.
You already know these six prefixes from unit 2: *sina*, *huna*, *hana*, *hatuna*, *hamna*, *hawana*. Exactly the same prefixes, attached to any verb.

The most common everyday examples: *sielewi* (I don't understand), *sijui* (I don't know), *sitaki* (I don't want), *sipendi* (I don't like), *sisemi* (I don't say). These five sentences alone will rescue many conversations.

grammars.title: Endings that don't change — and four short verbs
body: The "-a becomes -i" rule only applies to native Bantu verbs, which always end in *-a*. Verbs borrowed from Arabic end in *-i*, *-e* or *-u*, and **keep their ending as it is**.
after: The four short verbs in the lower rows keep *ku-* in positive sentences but **drop it in negative ones** — because the negative prefix is already long enough to carry the sound. *Ninakula* → *sili*. *Anakuja* → *haji*.

How to recognize them in a dictionary without memorizing: if the verb ends in **-a**, change it to **-i**. If it ends in any other letter, leave it alone. It's that simple, and there are no exceptions to memorize.
⚠️ *Kujua* (to know) ends in *-a*, so its negative is *sijui*, *hujui*, *hajui*. And you already know the negative of *kuwa na* (to have) from unit 2: *sina*, not *siwi*.

blocks.text: In East Africa, a direct refusal feels rude. The table below runs from the gentlest to the firmest — and the first three rows are the ones you'll need most.

head: Kiswahili
Say it
When to use it
rows: "Maybe later" — declining an invitation without closing the door
"I don't want any, thank you" — polite and clear

blocks.text: ⚠️ Note the difference between *hapana* and *siyo*. *Hapana* refuses a request ("want tea?" → "no"). *Siyo* denies a statement ("are you Malaysian?" → "no, I'm not"). Using *hapana* to deny also gets understood, but *siyo* sounds more accurate.

One lifesaver that isn't in the table yet: **Sijui** (I don't know). It is honest, it is polite, and it almost always gets answered with a long explanation that teaches you more than pretending to understand would.

sections.title: Kibanda cha chai — the stall and what's on it

head: Kiswahili
Say it
English
rows: sweet fried dough, like a doughnut

blocks.text: *Chai* in East Africa is not weak, plain tea. The default is *chai ya maziwa* — tea boiled together with milk, often with ginger (*tangawizi*) and cardamom. If you want plain tea without milk, ask for *chai ya rangi*, literally "tea of color" — tea that is only given its color, without milk.

*Mandazi* are a lightly spiced, slightly sweet fried dough, somewhere between a doughnut and a puffed pastry, and they are almost always on the table with morning tea. Ordering them in Swahili at any stall will make the seller smile.

exercises.prompt: Make these negative. Watch out: there are loan verbs and short verbs.
Choose the best reply: hapana, siyo, pole or samahani.
items: Your friend tells you her bag was lost. → ____
The seller offers sugar and you don't want any. → ____
You bump into someone at the market. → ____
You want to squeeze past in a narrow aisle. → ____
